practice.title: Act As If It's True
agreedSteps: Live each day as if death could come at any moment and any negative action could ripen into a lower rebirth. Let that shape every action, then check in at the end of the day: how did I do?

Notice when your behavior doesn't match your beliefs, not judgmentally but with curiosity. Ask why, and what it tells you about your understanding and faith. Even filling the water bowls is a chance to see it.
steps: Pick one teaching (death, lower rebirth, or continuity of consciousness) and make three columns: what I assert is true; how I actually live, looked at honestly; and what that shows me I actually believe.

Work on the gap with whichever tool fits: more familiarity, investigating the best argument for the opposite view, imagining what it would feel like to live the realization, strengthening faith in Buddha, acting as if it's true for a whole week, or finding the root belief that's blocking you.
Every time a moment, an hour, or a day passes, think: that is gone and I will never get it back.
Next class we'll do the traditional death meditation from The New Meditation Handbook: I will definitely die; day by day, moment by moment, my life is slipping away.
practice.quote: What would it be like this week to act as if this is true?

commentary.title: Don't Leave Doubts Unaddressed
content: Holding wrong views is the heaviest non-virtue: a firm decision that there are no enlightened beings, no karma, no past and future lives. As practitioners we probably don't hold that. But we still have doubts and confusion, or we're just not connected to some of these points, and we want to turn over the rocks and look at what's squirming underneath. Why is there a lack of conviction? Is it a seeing-is-believing bias? Some scientific materialism we absorbed from our culture?

It's interesting what we do believe in this world, including things with little or no proof, even things that are patently false, while things that are patently true are hard for us to believe. Unaddressed doubts don't stay neutral. When we're in a bad space they peek their head out and say, remember me? And they can harden into a wrong view.

Believing in something includes caring about its consequences. Believing in future lives isn't just an intellectual understanding of the continuity of consciousness. It means that future person matters, just as some past us paid it forward and gave us this mind-boggling good fortune. When my behavior doesn't line up with a teaching, I find it helpful to conclude not that something's wrong with me, but that I haven't gone deep enough on it yet.
commentary.quote: If we let them just sit there unaddressed, they're gonna rot away at our virtue.

commentary.title: Death in a Culture of Denial
content: Welcome to death week. Every one of our projects relates to death, because our delusions are rooted in attachment, and death meditation is the principal opponent to attachment other than actual renunciation. It's a meditation that does whatever we need it to do.

For most of human history death was everywhere: high infant mortality, bodies in the home, a generation that saw war up close. In much of modern life we've built a labyrinth of protection so we never have to face aging, sickness or death. That isn't normal for humankind, so we have to put in extra energy to expose our mind to it. When Geshe-la spends a page and a half on Gungtang's poem about old age, notice the urge to skip it. That urge is the denial we're working with.

Day by day, hour by hour, moment by moment, our life is passing. On our deathbed we'll want one more day with the people and practices we love, and those are exactly the days we're letting slip by now. Even good things like eating well or caring for the body can become a way of denying death. Caring for the vehicle we're using to reach liberation is fine; obsessing over it, or reaching for longevity fantasies, is an escape. The question is always: is this coming from denial of my death?
commentary.quote: It's a real kind of Swiss army knife of a meditation that kind of does whatever we need it to do.

commentary.title: Gentle Focus Compounds
content: Striving and pushing energy isn't actually focused on virtue. It comes from delusions like attachment and self-cherishing. A focused life is a gentle life that stays with virtue, like a broad, slow-flowing river, and the effects compound. The good things we've done begin to interconnect and support each other.

Thirty consecutive minutes of focused reading of a Dharma book (no phone, no article, no looking things up) builds on an exponential curve. It looks flat at first, then the mind gets deeper and even blissful. Five hours of ten minutes on, ten minutes off is probably net negative; the mind just feels jumbled.

A distracted mind never quiets down, never gets these compounding benefits, and ends up feeling lousy and burnt out. Death meditation helps cut through this: I may die today, so I don't want to chase that diversion.
commentary.quote: So if we can just stay on virtue, mentally, in a focused way, not striving, not pushing, then we'll definitely see beautiful and miraculous things arise.

commentary.title: Closing the Belief–Behavior Gap
content: Take death, lower rebirth, or the continuity of consciousness, and make three columns. One: what do I assert is true? Two: how do I actually live, my mental, verbal and physical behavior looked at objectively? Three: what does that show me about what I actually believe? Sometimes it lines up. Sometimes it's a little off, or mega off.

Then work on the gap. Maybe it's just familiarity, an easy problem solved with more mindfulness. Maybe investigate the best version of the opposite argument and refute it, which frees you to believe your side. Maybe imagine the experience of living the realization and admire it; often you discover you do have the meditation, you were just approaching it scholastically. Maybe many struggles are really one faith-in-Buddha issue, and upgrading that handles them all. Or act all week as if it's true, and see a Buddha image in your living room as a living Buddha.

Or look for the root belief behind the obstacle: rules are bad, pleasure is the source of happiness, if I were just validated I'd be happy, if I had enough security I'd be happy. Often dislodging one deeply held belief like that frees everything else to flow again.
commentary.quote: What does that show me about what I actually believe?

commentary.title: The Mind We Bring
content: Dharma practice is the mindset, not the outer action. In complicated situations it's easy to get focused on the outer solution, but the inner action is everything. Always check what mental attitude you're bringing.

The same goes for virtue. Virtue isn't the outer action; it's a state of mind coming from within. When we find the virtue in an activity (it's my love, my compassion, my patience) and then delight in it and celebrate it, that's the power of effort, and it's one of the main ways to stay light.
commentary.quote: Dharma practice isn't about doing things for someone or not doing things for someone. It's about the mindset we bring.

commentary.title: The People We Don't Like
content: There's a way to like every living being deeply, even if it isn't today. The list of people we can't stand is a barometer of the distance between us and a bodhisattva. Until we love them as much as we love our dearest child, we're not there yet, which makes them very useful: they show us the negativity we're projecting that we still need to work through.

That doesn't mean we have to spend time with everyone. We only have so much time. But we never want to cut anyone off in our heart, because they're the ones who will help us become enlightened. And when someone goes from unbearable to someone we delight in, we see it was just our mind that changed.
A systematic Lamrim practice already holds everything. We never need to interrupt it for something else; the practices we explore in this class all fold inside it.
commentary.quote: That list is the gap right between us and a bodhisattva.

commentary.title: Not Only on the Improve Train
content: Wanting to improve is a good impulse, but if we're only ever trying to improve, that's a burnout mindset: an achievement, perfectionist mindset that agitates the heart and never lets us rest or celebrate the good that's already there.

Everyone here is doing an incredible amount of good with their mind and heart, in how they treat people, how they practice, how they cherish the center, and how they try to be a human in a complicated world. Balance the wish to refine your practice with a clear, non-deluded pride in your good qualities. Karma takes time to ripen.

The same goes for unusual experiences in practice. Dreams and signs are hard to interpret. The reliable gauge is whether our delusions are decreasing, our virtues are increasing, and our mind is becoming calmer and more peaceful.
commentary.quote: We're never just only on the improve train.

commentary.title: Find the Commonalities
content: When we meet people of other faiths, in class or in our family, Geshe-la's advice is to find the commonalities and build a bridge. If someone says God is an all-knowing, loving force in the world, we can say that's how I relate to Buddha too, and be happy together. Even if we think someone has gone astray, attacking or debating their faith never helps.

In our own practice, though, we don't want to mix traditions in a way that obstructs our understanding. Later Shantideva refutes a permanent creator God, to help us understand dependent relationship and a more precise sense of Buddha. If we relate to Buddha as an omnipotent creator, contradictions arise: why do I suffer? With others, find the commonalities; with ourself, make sure no strange mixed view is getting in the way.
commentary.quote: No one responds to their faith being attacked, or debated with, no one.

commentary.title: Three Kinds of Tiredness
content: There's physical tiredness from real work, which usually leaves us feeling good about ourselves and needing rest. There's mental tiredness from using the mind a lot, and the answer is to use the mind in a way that's still virtuous but less taxing: mantras while lying down, listening to teachings, pujas, time with loved ones. And there's the modern kind, tiredness from dullness and apathy, which is really a lack of inspiration.

That third kind often comes from hedonism: searching for happiness in external things until the mind is so fried on novelty and stimulation that nothing has any luster. There's no outer solution. We have to cut the dullness at its cause by changing how we think, and bringing daily appearances into the path is our main way as Kadampas. Ask over and over, how is this teaching me Dharma? Even a curb can teach Dharma, and when everything teaches us, the heart is full.

Try to state your question in one or two sentences. Until we can, we haven't figured out what we're really asking. Revising it again and again often reveals the answer, or makes the question so clear that it can be answered.
commentary.quote: External things cannot give us joy. All they do is breed attachment and dissatisfaction.

dataShares: Suzanne stepped in on Cherishing Others Day to clear up a misunderstanding between a friend and someone she barely knew, instead of staying out of it. KK pointed to the inner mindset we bring as the real practice.

Dale has been following the Lamrim systematically without adding extra practices, and finds his concentration deepening and himself reaching out to new neighbors. KK affirmed that the Lamrim has everything in it.
Anne K met up with someone she had avoided for a year after reflecting on equanimity, had a great time, and resolved never to cut anyone off.
Fran has been practicing finding the virtue in each activity and delighting in it. KK connected this to joyful effort.
Mimi has been holding the long-term view and the broad, slow-flowing river, keeping her Dakini Yoga practice gentle, and feels much calmer.
David spent the week rejoicing in his practice instead of only focusing on areas to improve, which made practice more fun. He also asked about verse 21; KK said the commentary is coming.
Marianne shared a moment of being awed by someone's appearance and seeing her as a deity. KK suggested checking whether such experiences bring peace and accord with virtue.
Mimi asked how to respond when a family member questions the faith they grew up in. KK: with others, find the commonalities.
Anne K asked whether our behavior falls short because we don't believe, or because we don't care about our future self. KK: believing includes that care.
Ryan asked how to keep a good mind when he's drained by the end of the day. KK distinguished three kinds of tiredness and asked him to bring the question back in one sentence.
